items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Anyway, while Sarah Vaughan was singing, there was something I played behind her, which must have impressed her.

ctx.x: Stan Levey the drummer, and I said Red Rodney, and there may have been a couple of others. And they all came and they sat in with the Collegians. They must have liked the way we sound and they sat in with us. Sarah Vaughan sang, Billy Eckstine sang, Dexter played, Red Rodney sat back with the trumpet section and played, and Stan Levey played drums. There was a pianist too. I can’t remember his name, but he was known in the jazz field. Anyway, while Sarah Vaughan was singing, there was something I played behind…

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Quincy Jones commissioned me to do an album with Sarah Vaughan and there was a varied type of instrumental group there.

ctx.x: At the time it was playing whatever gig came my way, it was a club date by club date, I mean one of these square occasions where you play for people who dance with two left feet, and you had to play everything from “Hello Dolly” to “Mame” to whatever else squares like. And a lot of engagements where people come by and they pass by the band and they look up — oh there’s a bunch of waiters standing on stage. I mean that’s what the attitude — they don’t say this specifically, but that’s what it looks like they’re…

some clubs and at that time I was still getting writing assignments. I might write for — there was a time when I was hired to write for Frankie Lymon, and O.C. Smith hired me to do some writing for him. I did the writing for an Irene Reid recording session that was done with a big band, Quincy Jones commissioned me to do an album with Sarah Vaughan and there was a varied type of instrumental group there. items.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995
items.q: It was great working with him because he, like Sarah Vaughan, usually let me have free hand, free reign

ctx.x: Can you tell us about writing for Joe Williams? You wrote a certain style for him, and what it was like to work with him when he was with the band?

It was great working with him because he, like Sarah Vaughan, usually let me have free hand, free reign, and just let me have the lyrics and he’d sing them down for me, and give me an idea of basically the kind of backing he wanted, and let me go myself from there. ‘Cause I used to pride myself on being able to really write some Basie type blues.
